canberra.title: Coalition promises biggest cut to migration in Australia’s history
canberra.snippet: The Coalition has vowed to deliver the largest cut to immigration in Australian history, reducing overseas migration numbers to 100,000 f...
canberra.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor wants to cut 650,000 temporary visa holders over four years. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The Coalition has vowed to deliver the largest cut to immigration in Australian history, reducing overseas migration numbers to 100,000 for two years and slashing a massive 650,000 temporary visa holders over four years.

Angus Taylor released the Opposition’s long-awaited migration policy on Tuesday (6 October), saying he would “take back control” of the system and protect the Australian way of life.

The Opposition Leader said a future government led by him and Nationals leader Matt Canavan would deliver a budget-neutral outcome, free up more homes for Australians, and take pressure off frontline services.

“Under Labor, the numbers have been too high, and the standards have been too low. This has been a disaster for Australia,” Mr Taylor said.

“A Liberals and Nationals government I lead will deliver a migration program which puts Australians first.

“We need skilled migration, not mass migration. We will prioritise migrants with the skills Australia needs, who share our values and are committed to contributing to our country.

“This is about building the nation we want Australia to be. A fair system that puts our national interest first, that Australians can have confidence in, and that migrants can be proud of.

“Migration should strengthen our economy, fill critical skills gaps and help build a better Australia. It should not put further pressure on housing and essential services or leave Australians worse off.”

The Liberal leader said he would ensure a “laser focus” on the skills Australia needs when it comes to issuing skilled working visas.

“The Liberals and Nationals have fixed Labor’s migration mess before, and will fix it again,” he said.

The Coalition plan is to reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 a year for the first two years, before levelling out at around 160,000 in year four.

At 100,000 a year, net overseas migration would be the lowest outside the pandemic since 2004, and about the sustained level of the late 1990s.

After four years, the plan would maintain the migration rate as a share of the population below the average under the Howard government.

It would reduce the stock of temporary visa holders by about 650,000 over four years, while keeping the permanent skilled migration program capped at 185,000 places a year.

In the longer term, the cap on the permanent program would be reduced if necessary to keep migration below housing completions and align with the Coalition’s migration and housing pledge.

The Coalition would also abolish temporary graduate visas and reduce international student migration by restricting most secondary applicants.

PhD, health and education graduates or those at regional universities would have access to post-study transitional visas.

International student commencements would be cut to 240,000.

Senator Canavan said Australia needed a migration system that put Australian workers first, not one that relied on mass migration.

“Labor has let too many people into our country,” he said.

“Labor’s mass migration has pushed down wages, hurt living standards and led to a temporary guest worker class that is eroding our social harmony.

“It is unAustralian to rely on cheap foreign labour to boost our economic performance like Labor is doing.

“We will restore the traditional, Australian approach to migration which targets the skills we need without undermining a fair go for Australian workers.

“We’re not just a campground, we are a nation of borders, we’re not a booking.com site, and we owe Australians a living wage, not to have their salaries undermined by a cheap foreign labour force.”

Last month, Labor unveiled its planned migration system changes, which include international students no longer being able to easily bring their families to Australia; a clampdown on visa-hopping; and visas for skilled migrant workers in teaching, construction and agriculture being given priority.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has claimed credit for the Coalition’s migration policy and Labor’s recent announcement, saying she started the whole debate.

Her plan is to cut net overseas migration by 750,000 over three years.

“Liberal and Labor have both been dragged kicking and screaming into the immigration debate by One Nation,” Senator Hanson posted on social media.

“They’ve ignored Australians for decades on this issue and they’d prefer it if they didn’t have to talk about it at all.”

Independent MP Monique Ryan has quickly criticised the Coalition’s migration policy, however, warning that Australia was at risk of importing the fear and division that characterised debate about immigration in the US and parts of Europe.

“The race to the bottom on immigration is well and truly on between the Liberals and One Nation,” Dr Ryan said.

“Today’s savage cuts by Angus Taylor show that the country’s conservative parties are in lockstep on divisive, harmful policies which scapegoat the migrant communities vital to Australia’s economic and cultural future.”

canberra.title: Army veteran jailed for sexually abusing girls aged 10 and 14
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse. A long-term member of the Australian Defence Force with decades of service in the Ar...
canberra.content:
The 74-year-old man served in the Australian Army for nearly 25 years before retiring due to his charges. Photo: ADF.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse.

A long-term member of the Australian Defence Force with decades of service in the Army has been jailed for sexually abusing a 14-year-old girl he met through his tennis club, as well as his 10-year-old step-granddaughter.

The 74-year-old man was seen leaning forwards and staring intently at the judge in the ACT Supreme Court on Tuesday (6 October), where he was sentenced to seven years’ jail with effectively five years’ non-parole.

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum said he was 60 when he met the first girl through his tennis club in the early 2010s.

She was 14 at the time and her mother was a single parent, so she accepted the help when the man offered to give her daughter lifts to tennis.

But the girl said he then ingratiated himself into her life, offering to give her private tennis classes, then private driving lessons.

He started internet accounts to communicate with her, claiming he wanted to share his “spiritual teachings” with her.

“As I hope to demonstrate, that explanation is frankly ridiculous,” Chief Justice McCallum said.

The man told the girl they were “harmonious spirits” who had known each other for thousands of years. He said “sex is neither right or wrong”, “a man and a girl having sex” was “just an event” and they could “easily be more than friends”.

He told her he taught sex, had sexual students and wrote pornographic stories. He also asked if she watched pornography herself.

“Such is the nature of his ‘spiritual teachings’,” Chief Justice McCallum said.

In addition, the man sent the girl an indecent video, the contents of which the judge described as “completely depraved”.

During their driving lessons, he took her into remote areas like the Namadgi National Park and indecently assaulted her on three occasions, until she summoned the courage to tell him to stop and ended their interactions. Despite this, he kept trying to speak to her.

This was not the last child the man abused.

In the early 2020s, he started trying to sexualise the relationship he had with his step-granddaughter, who was aged 10 at the time.

For instance, he told her about different kinds of kissing and how they had been lovers in another life.

“That was an appalling thing for a grandfather to say to a little girl,” Chief Justice McCallum said.

They were driving in his car when he stopped at a red light and asked the girl for “a lover’s kiss”. He then kissed her on at least two occasions in the car.

They were also at his home when he invited her into his study and kissed her again.

“It must have been truly disgusting for the victim,” Chief Justice McCallum said.

The man has had two children with his long-term wife, including the step-parent of his step-granddaughter.

He served in the Australian Army for 23 years.

Chief Justice McCallum said he had shown no empathy or remorse for his offending.

She noted that he was reluctant to discuss his offending with the author of a pre-sentence report, claiming this was due to legal advice and ongoing appeals.

The author thought he consistently minimised, justified and denied his actions.

Due to time served, the man, who is not named to protect his victims’ identities, will be eligible to be released on parole in May 2031.

He was found guilty of nine charges at a jury trial earlier this year, including two counts of the persistent sexual abuse of a child.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Murder squad investigates suspicious death of man in Watson
canberra.snippet: After police discovered a man’s body at his north Canberra home, the homicide squad announced they believe he died in suspicious ci...
canberra.content:
6 October 2026

Start the conversation

Police have found the body of a man at his home on Hanson Place, Watson. Photo: John Lomnicki.

After police discovered a man’s body at his north Canberra home, the homicide squad announced they believe he died in suspicious circumstances.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said police were asked to check on the welfare of a 70-year-old man on Monday morning (5 October).

A short time later, officers arrived at his home on Hanson Place, Watson, where they sadly discovered his body inside the residence.

“A crime scene was established and after enquiries over the past 24 hours by the homicide squad, the death is now being treated as suspicious,” the police spokesperson said.

Police want anyone who saw suspicious activity in or near Hanson Place in the days before Monday to come forward.

Police also asked anyone with dash-cam or CCTV footage of the immediate area to contact them.

Hanson Place is a small cul-de-sac off Higinbotham Street, near the Watson shops.

If you can assist police, provide them with your contact details via the Crime Stoppers ACT website by clicking here, quoting 8518788.

canberra.title: Blaze destroys much of former Bay Waters Hotel
canberra.snippet: About “60 per cent” of the former Bay Waters Hotel building has been destroyed in an overnight blaze. A Fire and Rescue NSW s...
canberra.content:
6 October 2026

Start the conversation

The former motel site, in Batemans Bay, was also damaged by fire in 2023. Photo: Fire and Rescue NSW Station 384 Moruya Facebook.

About “60 per cent” of the former Bay Waters Hotel building has been destroyed in an overnight blaze.

A Fire and Rescue NSW spokesperson said multiple units were called to the site on Old Punt Road in North Batemans Bay at about 9:15 pm last night (5 October).

About eight units were present, with NSW Rural Fire Service assisting.

Firefighters took up a “defensive position” and checked the building to see if anyone was inside.

The spokesperson said that while they were able to contain the blaze, about “60 per cent” of the building was destroyed.

Firefighters were forced to retreat when part of the building’s roof collapsed.

A NSW Police spokesperson said officers from South Coast Police District had established a crime scene and started making inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the fire.

“Scene of crime officers and fire investigators are expected to examine the location in daylight in an effort to determine the cause of the blaze,” the spokesperson said.

Fire and Rescue NSW have returned to the site today (6 October) as their investigation continues.

The state bought the site for $4 million in 2018 as an ongoing motel business as part of the Batemans Bay bridge works.

As only a portion of the land was required, the balance – which included the motel building – remained under licence to the operator.

As of late 2023, it was being used as accommodation for about 20 homeless people.

After Transport for NSW (TfNSW) received advice that the building’s structure had been compromised, a decision was made to end a month-to-month lease arrangement with the third-party operator leasing the site.

Two months after the June 2023 blaze, the property became unsafe to live in, meaning the tenants had to be evicted.

The former Bay Waters Hotel was purchased in 2018 by the NSW Government. Photo: Fire and Rescue NSW Station 384 Moruya Facebook.

Region understands TfNSW took back possession of the property in 2025, with the site now secured.

In early 2026, a TfNSW spokesperson told Region that discussions around how the site could be utilised were ongoing.

“Transport is working with other NSW Government agencies to provide access to the property to explore future uses for this property,” they said at the time.

Region has contacted Member for Bega Doctor Michael Holland and TfNSW for comment.

As police inquiries are ongoing, anyone with information is asked to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Reduced Capital Circle speed limit, no more bridge expansion: the new plans for light rail stage 2B revealed
canberra.snippet: New track arrangements, more kiss-and-ride stops and reduced speed limits are some of the changes made in the final environmental impact ...
canberra.content:
The final environmental impact statement documents see light rail stage 2B going under parts of Commonwealth Ave. Photo: ACT Government.

New track arrangements, more kiss-and-ride stops and reduced speed limits are some of the changes made in the final environmental impact documents for light rail stage 2B.

It only assesses the State Circle East alignment – a route that was confirmed by the ACT Government in May.

One major change is that the Melrose Drive Bridge over Yarralumla Creek will no longer be widened by about 7.5 metres (to accommodate extra southbound traffic) during stage 2B’s construction.

The impact of such construction works was a key concern raised in community submissions, including potential safety risks and the increased use of, or shortcutting by motorists through, nearby roads such as Theodore Street.

“Construction of these works would have likely required all traffic between Melrose Drive and Yarra Glen to be temporarily redirected to Launceston Street, Theodore Street or drivers would have to alter their route entirely,” the documents stated.

Extra traffic modelling was undertaken to see what other options were available outside of widening the bridge. Conservative 2041 traffic forecasts showed road performance (including queuing along Melrose Drive toward the Theodore Street intersection) would be similar when comparing the bridge-widening option with an alternative design that shifted the lane configuration further south.

In light of the findings, the bridge widening is no longer proposed.

“This change will avoid the need to close sections of Melrose Drive and Yarra Glen completely during construction while achieving similar traffic outcomes when the project is operational.”

An additional aspect is the proposed reduced speed limit for parts of Capital Circle.

After the draft EIS exhibition period, further design reviews identified a traffic safety risk at the crossing between Capital Circle and Adelaide Avenue.

The final documents have proposed several posted speed limit changes for roads in the Commonwealth Avenue, Parliament House and Inner South precincts.

“[The changes create] a more predictable environment through the transition from Capital Circle to Adelaide Avenue, and promote awareness and visibility through the curve,” the documents stated.

No posted speed limit changes were suggested for the Yarra Glen or Woden precincts.

Changes to posted speed limits for light rail stage 2B. Photo: ACT Government.

Other additions include more kiss-and-ride spaces at the Hopetoun Circuit, Kent Street and Carruthers Street stops; lighting installation along the active travel path on the eastern side of Yarralumla Creek; improvements to accessibility and connectivity at the Kent Street and Carruthers Street stops; consideration of a Customer Service Officer facility at the Phillip Oval stop; more construction compound sites; and an extra track cross-over on Commonwealth Avenue after the Albert Hall stop.

As previously announced, a major design change has been made for the track along State Circle, between Commonwealth Avenue and Adelaide Avenue, from a ‘median running’ arrangement to an ‘inner running’ arrangement between Sydney Avenue and Adelaide Avenue.

“This moves the proposed light rail infrastructure, including the Melbourne Avenue stop, from the median of State Circle to the inner verge on the Capital Hill side,” the documents stated.

This would mean State Circle would no longer need to be widened past Sydney Avenue, motorists would still be able to turn right to access the Presbyterian Church of St Andrew, and the existing street parking and loading zone on State Circle between Hobart Avenue and west of Melbourne Avenue would remain.

The left slip lanes would be removed at the Sydney Avenue intersection.

“This will help to retain existing parking arrangements and reduce disruption to nearby residents, businesses and the road network.”

The final EIS documents include a switch to an inner track arrangement on State Circle, south of Sydney Avenue. Photo: ACT Government.

The covered section between Commonwealth Avenue and State Circle remains in the final documents.

The 125-metre-long section under the southbound carriageway of Commonwealth Avenue would emerge on State Circle without disrupting southbound traffic on Commonwealth Avenue.

How this would be achieved depends on further investigation and consultation.

“Any alternative solution would balance factors including traffic and road network performance, urban design and visual impacts, and heritage considerations,” the documents stated.

Artist impressions show how light rail stage 2B could fit into Canberra's landscape. Photo: ACT Government.

Both the Commonwealth and ACT Governments must now consider the EIS and decide whether the project can proceed and, if so, under what conditions.

This decision is expected by the end of the year.

If the environmental approval process is cleared, detailed design work will then need to begin to support planning approvals, including a Works Approval from the National Capital Authority and a development approval from the Territory Planning Authority (TPA).

Parts of the project within the Parliamentary Zone will also require approval from both Houses of Parliament.

“Once planning approvals are complete, Infrastructure Canberra will develop a detailed business case to inform government investment decisions,” the documents stated.

“This ensures funding and delivery decisions are based on a clearly defined scope and detailed investigations. There will be more opportunities to have your say on the project as it progresses through these next steps.”

australia.title: PM called on to act on communal grave revelations as NSW commits to urgent review
australia.snippet: ‘All deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,’ authorities say after Gua...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has been urged to use national cabinet to stop the use of unmarked communal graves to bury impoverished Australians and address failings that are leaving family and friends blindsided.

Guardian Australia’s revelations on Tuesday that unmarked, communal graves were being used, in some cases without notifying the families of the deceased, prompted widespread political condemnation on Tuesday, including from federal Liberal MPs, state Labor ministers, and the Greens.

The New South Wales government committed to an urgent review of the practice.

The health minister, Ryan Park, said he had not been previously aware of the way the graves were being used by his government.

He has tasked his department to explore reforms, including emulating the Victorian model, where individuals are buried with their own plot and marking, a process that costs just $3,000 per funeral.

“I think it’s something that we need to do better,” Park said. “Quite clearly, the dignity of those who have … passed, as well as for their families, is something that we need to take into consideration, and we need to do this better.”

Independent senator David Pocock urged Albanese to raise the issue at national cabinet and seek a uniform agreement across states and territories to ensure dignified burials and a basic standard of notification to families, friends, and others associated with the deceased.

“Being poor in a country as wealthy as Australia should not condemn you to an unmarked communal grave,” he said.

“While I appreciate that this may not be at the top of most people’s list of daily concerns, how we treat our most vulnerable, including in death, goes to our values and who we are as a country.”

Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers, people with gambling addictions and migrants from developing countries have been buried together at Rookwood cemetery in western Sydney, with each plot often holding between four and six unrelated people.

Shadow minister for defence personnel Phillip Thompson described the burials of war veterans as “deeply concerning”.

“I am disappointed to hear Australian veterans are among those being buried in unmarked mass graves,” Thompson said. “These men and women served our nation and deserve dignity, respect in death, regardless of their financial circumstances.”

He said it was the job of the federal government to ensure every veteran is identified and appropriately commemorated.

NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson called on the NSW government to urgently examine whether its model for identifying the friends and family of deceased persons had “the people, resources and safeguards” necessary.

“Matters of grief, death and human dignity cannot be treated as administrative burdens to be processed at the lowest possible cost,” she said. “Nobody should receive a lesser measure of humanity in death simply because they died without money.”

In at least six cases identified by the Guardian, friends, families, homelessness charities and community leaders had not been informed about the process, denying them a chance to intervene and pay for alternative funeral arrangements, a likely breach of NSW Health policy.

‘Unacceptable’

Park has accepted that past failings are “unacceptable” and NSW Health has apologised, acknowledging that it has not always treated those without financial means with the dignity and respect they are entitled to.

“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a NSW Health Pathology spokesperson said.

“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”

NSW Health also said it is “committed to changing the way we work”. That includes reforms to better work with loved ones, funeral service providers and partner agencies to “assess and manage deceased persons without financial means”.

The government has also signalled greater cooperation with community and charity groups to seek funeral funding, after the Guardian revealed at least 18 people known to homelessness services had been buried in unmarked and communal graves without the sector’s knowledge.

The rules require the government to do whatever it can to contact family, friends and others associated with the deceased before burying or cremating them, to check if they want to fund alternative funerals.

Who is responsible?

Responsibility for that process had been shared between NSW Health and police until 2025. Reforms last year gave NSW Health Pathology responsibility for the process when deaths occurred in the community or in cases before the coroner, replacing police.

Park said the changes made since 2025 were significant in establishing a more “person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve”.

“Losing a loved one is never easy, and everyone should be treated with dignity and respect when they pass, regardless of their financial circumstances,” Park said.

“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable.”

Independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich welcomed changes made by NSW Health to address the problem. “Those who are marginalised and vulnerable in our community deserve the opportunity to be farewelled respectfully, honouring the life they lived,” he said.

Guardian Australia’s investigation has identified serious failings in burials that occurred this year, after the 2025 reforms. That includes the case of Peter Giesel, a Sydney man who died in 2024 and was buried in an unmarked communal grave in June without the knowledge of his sister, Nicole, or close friend Elaine Grady.

NSW Health said it had updated its policy to require “the provision of a uniform flat grave marker for people who have been buried”.

Despite this, burials have continued to occur without any marker.

The operator of Rookwood, Metropolitan Memorial Parks, says the state government has not funded it to provide grave markings.

australia.title: Coalition’s migration plan risks breaching India free trade agreement and damaging economy, advocates warn
australia.snippet: Angus Taylor’s drastic cuts to graduate visas aim to end a citizenship pathway, but universities body says changes will make Australia le...
australia.content:
The Coalition’s migration plan risks breaching Australia’s free trade agreement with India, signed by the former Morrison government, allowing Indian students to stay and work for up to four years after completing their studies.

Angus Taylor on Tuesday announced plans to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for the first two years of a Coalition government and up to 160,000 in year four, in a plan which would abolish temporary graduate visas, make major cuts to international student, bridging and temporary protection visas, and halve humanitarian places.

Under the plan, temporary graduate visas would be slashed from 271,200 to just 10,000 by 2031-32.

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said any graduate wanting to remain in Australia would have to return home and apply for a separate temporary visa.

“Universities and other educational institutions have reverted to, sadly, selling a pathway to some form of permanency or perhaps even citizenship rather than education; that’s not what this scheme was set up for,” Duniam said.

“Abolishing the temporary graduate visa … means we can focus on skills we need in this country, not just whatever is churned out of our universities.”

Duniam said there would be a four-year transitional phase before the abolition of the temporary graduate visa. Some workers in priority areas such as health, education and in some regional areas would be allowed to remain.

Phil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), said this could breach the India free trade agreement.

A letter on the agreement, from the then Liberal trade minister Dan Tehan, in April 2022, states: “Australia agrees to maintain the following opportunities for former students to live, study and work in Australia temporarily after finishing their studies.” This includes allowing trade or diploma graduates to stay up to 18 months, bachelor graduates up to two years, bachelor graduates in Stem courses and master’s graduates up to three years, and doctoral degree graduates up to four years.

Honeywood said it was “ironic” the Coalition was targeting the visa when it had negotiated special conditions with India, the second largest cohort of international students in Australia, behind China.

He warned Australia would lose skilled workers in critical areas under the Coalition’s changes.

He said Australia would take “money off bright young people for their qualifications” before sending them home without having the chance to benefit from their high-demand health, IT and engineering skills.

Honeywood said the explosion in non-genuine international students coming to Australia was in part due to a post-Covid directive by the then Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison, who increased the number of hours international students could work in key industries.

“[Morrison] opened the floodgates to non-genuine students coming out of Covid without consulting the sector, promising more work rights for international students while they were meant to study full-time,” Honeywood said.

A Coalition spokesperson told Guardian Australia there would be no treaty breach, and the party would look at establishing different visa pathways for some of those graduates.

“Our treaty commitments are to provide temporary visa pathways for some students to stay post their study for short periods. Which visas are provided is up to Australia,” the spokesperson said.

“When we implement this policy in government we will work through with affected international partners which new visa pathways, including skilled visa pathways, their citizens can access.”

The Coalition’s plan would cut international student commencements to 240,000, below the current planning level of 295,000. But a spokesperson for the assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said the sector was now tracking towards 250,000 commencements for this calendar year.

Universities Australia said the changes risked doing “lasting damage” to Australia’s higher education sector and the economy. In a statement, its chief executive, Luke Sheehy, said removing the temporary graduate program could make Australia less attractive for students.

“Restricting post-study work rights also risks making Australia less competitive for talented students and graduates at precisely the time we need more skilled people contributing to our economy.”

Hill said removing the temporary graduate visa would make Australia a less attractive option and deny the country the ability to “select the brightest skilled graduates and would hurt Australian employers and industry”.

He said all comparable nations had competitive postgraduate work opportunities.

“Wiping out temporary graduate visas would mean many of the brightest students will simply never choose Australia, further trashing our fourth biggest export.”

australia.title: Australia faces summer of extreme weather, Anthony Albanese warns at pre-Cop
australia.snippet: Prime minister tells delegates in Tuvalu and Fiji that ‘super El Niño’ brewing in the Pacific shows climate change is ‘here right now’ An...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has warned Australia faces a hazardous summer, likely including floods, cyclones and extreme heat, due to the immediate threat of the climate change and a rising “super El Niño”.

Speaker alongside national leaders at a climate summit in Fiji, the prime minister said the expected nasty summer and the demonstrated impact on Pacific island countries – including low-lying Tuvalu – showed the world could not afford to let the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C “just slip from our grasp”.

“Climate change is not a problem for the future. It is here right now, and we know that sea levels here in the western Pacific are rising at more than twice the global average. We know also that the forecast of super El Niño may test us all,” he said

“In Australia, we are expecting a summer of floods, of cyclones, of extreme heat, and extreme behaviour…The science told us that if we didn’t act to address global emissions this is precisely what would occur, and tragically that is playing out.”

Albanese’s comments came after a delegation of national and global agency leaders visited Tuvalu to see the impact of the climate crisis on one of the countries most at risk. A collection of three reef islands and six atolls, Tuvalu is home to about 10,000 people and mostly less than 2 metres above sea level.

The visit was promised by the Albanese government last year as part of a compromise deal when it missed out on hosting the Cop31 climate conference. Cop31 will be in Turkey next month; Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting a preparatory meeting.

Tuvalu was wet and grey for the visit, and the capital of Funafuti – spectacular from the air on a clear day – was visible only in strips between heavy rain clouds during descent.

After a cultural welcome and a tour of a climate resilience project, leaders held a “sautalaga” meeting – an exchange of views – where they expressed support for the country and urged more rapid action to cut emissions and provide island states with the money needed to adapt.

The delegation heard from Melelusi Sokotia, a 13-year-old local student, who said her friends dreamed of “becoming teachers, doctors, builders” but spent their lives wondering if their island would survive into their adult lives. “We all have one single dream: to grow safely here in Tuvalu,” she said. “We are not asking for peace. We are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”

Tuvalu’s prime minister, Feleti Teo, stressed island states needed faster access to global climate finance to deal with worsening extreme events. “Why should countries like Tuvalu take on more debt to protect ourselves from a climate crisis we did so little to cause? We should not have to borrow our way out of a crisis.”

The Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said the world was on the brink of overshooting the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C – agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and must bring forward plans to cut emissions. “That is not radical. It is in line with our agreement, our obligation, and the scientific reality,” he said. “The transition away from fossil fuels was agreed to by all of us in Dubai [at the Cop28 summit in 2023]. It is not a new ask, and it is not open for renegotiation.”

Australia has faced criticism at the talks for arguing for greater climate action while continuing to new expanded coal and gas developments. An Australian state regulator last week approved a major coalmine development that would be the largest in New South Wales’ history if it receives federal approval.

Albanese, attending his first UN climate conference as prime minister since his election in 2022, said a message from the Tuvalu trip was that “climate change must be understood as being something more than about science or targets”. “It must be understood that effectively it’s about people,” he said.

The delegation, which include former Australian prime minister Julia Gillard, now the chair of health charity Wellcome, were shown a land reclamation project to extend the atoll by about 20 hectares using sand and gravel dredged from its lagoon.

Tuvalu’s director of climate change, Jamie Ovia, told the visitors sea level rise was projected to increase the annual cost of damage from flooding and storm surges to US$34m a year by 2050 and $63m – more than Tuvalu’s GDP – by 2100.

He said the coastal fishing catch could be reduced by 16% and tuna stocks worth $4m a year could be lost as seas warmed. “We need time to adapt,” Ovia said. “Tuvalu is doing our part. Will you act with Tuvalu and will you act in time?”

australia.title: OpenAI delivers a mea culpa to the Australian government in person – but answers still elude
australia.snippet: Jason Kwon’s answers were provided in a helpful, quiet and calm manner. For a company under intense scrutiny, there were no missteps Open...
australia.content:
Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare.

Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making.

In other words, just like ChatGPT.

Even the content of his responses evoked the AI assistant he was there to defend.

Asked by Pocock “why did you send an email to an arbitrary department email?” Kwon replied: “In retrospect, we should have done what you’re suggesting”. Asked why Altman wasn’t informed before his meeting with Marles, and why the company didn’t fess up there, Kwon said: “I agree the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better”.

One couldn’t help but be reminded of the way the chatbot responds when pulled up on a mistake: “Good catch. You’re right to push back. My bad, that one’s on me.”

In Kwon’s parlance, the models – built from the ground up by OpenAI, which reportedly wants to value itself at $1.4tn – “accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to.” He tried to explain that the “novelty” of this incident meant the company had “learned our lesson”, which was that it should inform victims of such incidents much earlier, rather than waiting.

Kwon again apologised for the company only sending a casual email to the federal government disclosing that its agent had inappropriately accessed Medicare statistics, but tried to explain to Tuesday’s parliamentary hearing that it was sometimes “difficult” to figure how to make such notifications to a big sprawling public service.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Senator David Pocock helpfully offered: “I assume someone in your government relations team has mobile phone numbers of ministers and various people?”

There was a similar air of post-facto contrition as Kwon – OpenAI’s chief strategy officer – could offer few answers about why the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, didn’t inform the Australian deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, about the incident when they met face-to-face in San Francisco on 1 September. That was nine days before the company emailed Services Australia, and nearly a whole month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.

Kwon said Altman wasn’t aware of the incident before the Marles meeting. After today’s committee hearing, it’s still unclear why.

It’s a big government, and maybe Kwon is right that it’s “difficult” to find the right person to talk to. But some could also argue that your boss shaking hands with Australia’s deputy prime minister would be something of a useful window.

At least, we learned, he said the company didn’t use AI to write the infamous email. Small blessings that they managed to ask a human to write the email – even if it went to an obscure inbox.

But with Australia actually striving to become a tech capital for datacentres and AI – as the revolving door of big tech companies told the inquiry, from Anthropic to Microsoft and Google – then setting the basic rules of the road for these firms, about how they must act and respond to this country and its government, is critical.

Kwon said OpenAI was committed to providing future notifications “very quickly”, and that there were no further incidents they were aware of. But he casually dropped in one staggering fact: OpenAI was still trawling through the activity logs for the agents involved in the Services Australia breach, with those logs totalling 50 petabytes of data.

A petabyte is 1,000 terabytes, or 1 million gigabytes.

Kwon made the mind-boggling claim that it would take a human 66m years – never sleeping, never resting – to go through that data by hand.

The team tasked with checking Services Australia’s email inboxes must be hoping there aren’t any more dramas lurking in there.

world.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
world.snippet: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebo...
world.content:
Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.

This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.

A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.

The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.

Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.

He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).

Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.

He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.

Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.

Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.

After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.

The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.

The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.

“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”

The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.

Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”

North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

world.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
world.snippet: Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again As renewed fighting has thr...
world.content:
As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.

The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.

Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.

The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.

Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.

Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.

“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.

“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”

In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.

Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.

“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”

Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.

“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.

The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.

Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”

Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.

Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.

An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.

* Names have been changed to protect their identities

world.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
world.snippet: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underw...
world.content:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.

Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.

After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.

Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.

“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.

“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”

On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.

She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.

“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

world.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
world.snippet: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeopl...
world.content:
Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.

The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.

Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”

The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.

But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.

Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.

“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century,” Campbell told the Guardian, but she said this was the first study to look at trauma and cause of death while examining human remains from the tombs.

Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.

Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.

The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.

“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”

Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.

Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.

She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”

Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.

“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

world.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
world.snippet: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has...
world.content:
An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.

Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.

“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”

The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.

Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.

The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.

More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.

The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.

The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.

This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.

While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”

Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.

Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.
